title: Onyx — Self-Hosted Open-Source ChatGPT / Claude Replacement
guide_markdown:
# Onyx — Self-Hosted Open-Source ChatGPT / Claude Replacement

**GitHub:** https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx
**Stars:** ~26,100
**License:** MIT (Community Edition); Enterprise Edition is source-available with paid add-ons
**Stack:** Python (~63%), TypeScript (~31%), Go (~2%)
**Repo path:** `repos/onyx/` (clone pending — sandbox blocked git clone in this session; run `git clone https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx.git repos/onyx` manually)

---

## What it is

Onyx (formerly Danswer) is the most mature open-source "ChatGPT for your company" you can actually self-host in a weekend. It's a full application layer on top of LLMs that ships with:

- A polished chat UI (multi-user, rooms, saved chats, custom personas)
- Agentic RAG over your own documents with hybrid vector + keyword indexing
- 50+ first-party connectors that crawl SaaS tools (Slack, Notion, Google Drive, Confluence, Jira, Gmail, GitHub, Salesforce, etc.) and keep them synced
- Pluggable LLM backends — Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OR fully local via Ollama / vLLM / LiteLLM
- Deep Research mode (ranked top on their internal leaderboard as of early 2026)
- Web search, code execution sandboxes, voice mode, image generation, MCP actions
- Custom Agents ("Assistants") with configurable instructions, tools, and knowledge scopes

It's basically the piece of infrastructure you'd build yourself if you wanted a personal/team knowledge layer that indexes everything you touch and lets an LLM agent search, reason, and act across it — but someone already built it, productized it, and open-sourced the core under MIT.

## How it works

Onyx is a classic modern RAG stack, but thoughtfully assembled:

**Ingestion layer**
- Connectors are Python modules that pull documents from sources on a schedule
- Each document gets chunked, cleaned, metadata-enriched, and embedded
- Embeddings are stored in a Vespa-based vector + keyword hybrid index (they previously used Typesense/others; Vespa is the current default)
- Access-control metadata is tracked per-document so permission boundaries are respected at query time

**Query layer**
- User query goes through an agentic planner (the "agent search" loop)
- Planner can decompose the question, run multiple sub-retrievals, chain web search + internal RAG, execute code in a sandbox, and call tools/MCP actions
- Retrieved chunks are reranked, filtered by permissions, and stuffed into the LLM prompt with citations
- The LLM backend is whatever you configure — cloud (Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini) or local (Ollama/vLLM)

**Infrastructure**
- **Postgres** for metadata, users, chat history
- **Vespa** (default) for the hybrid search index
- **Redis** for caching and rate limiting
- **Celery** workers for background jobs (indexing, connector syncs, reranking)
- **MinIO** (S3-compatible) for blob storage (uploaded files, attachments)
- **Model servers** — separate containers that run embedding + reranker + optional local LLM
- **Nginx** in front of the Next.js frontend and FastAPI backend

There's a **Lite mode** that strips the heavy search stack and runs as just a chat UI with BYO LLM, fitting in under 1 GB RAM. That's the right starting point if you just want "ChatGPT UI for my local Ollama" and will add RAG later.

## Connectors (highlights)

Onyx ships with 50+ connectors; the commonly useful ones for a personal/power-user setup:

- **Knowledge & docs:** Notion, Confluence, Google Drive, Dropbox, Box, OneDrive, S3, local file upload, generic web crawler, sitemap
- **Chat & communication:** Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, Gmail, Outlook
- **Dev tools:** GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Jira, Linear, Asana, ClickUp, Productboard
- **CRM / support:** Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk, Freshdesk, Intercom, Gong
- **Databases / BI:** Airtable, Mixpanel, generic SQL, Google Sheets
- **Media / code:** YouTube transcripts, ReadTheDocs, Sharepoint, Axero
- **Generic:** Requests-based web crawler, file upload, MCP actions for everything else

Each connector handles auth (OAuth, API key, service account), incremental sync, deletion propagation, and ACL metadata.

## LLM backend options

Onyx doesn't lock you in:

- **Cloud:** Anthropic (Claude family), OpenAI (GPT-4/5), Google Gemini, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock
- **Self-hosted:** Ollama (easy), vLLM (fast, GPU-hungry), LiteLLM proxy (universal adapter)
- **Embeddings:** Defaults to a local sentence-transformers model running in a sidecar; can swap for OpenAI/Cohere/Voyage
- **Rerankers:** Local cross-encoder or hosted (Cohere Rerank)

You can mix: cheap local embeddings + Claude for final synthesis is a great config. Routing per-assistant is supported — one assistant uses Claude, another uses a local Mistral.

## System requirements

**Full Onyx (production / power user):**
- Docker + Docker Compose
- 16 GB RAM minimum (32 GB recommended once you turn on reranker + local embedding)
- ~20 GB disk for the stack + whatever your document corpus demands
- GPU optional — only needed if you want a local LLM via vLLM. Embeddings are CPU-fine.

**Lite mode:**
- Docker + Compose
- ~1 GB RAM
- Any BYO LLM endpoint

**OS:** Linux is the blessed path; macOS/Windows via Docker Desktop works but is heavier.

## Quick start (Docker self-host)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx.git
cd onyx/deployment/docker_compose

# Copy and edit env vars (at minimum: set an LLM provider key
# or point GEN_AI_API_ENDPOINT at your Ollama)
cp .env.template .env
$EDITOR .env

# Boot the full stack
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d

# Wait ~2 minutes for model servers and Vespa to warm up
# Then hit http://localhost:3000 and create the admin account
```

Key env vars to know:
- `AUTH_TYPE` — `disabled` / `basic` / `google_oauth` / `oidc`
- `GEN_AI_MODEL_PROVIDER` and matching API key — or point at a local endpoint
- `INDEX_BATCH_SIZE` — tune for your RAM
- `POSTGRES_*`, `VESPA_*`, `REDIS_*` — default internal containers work fine

For Lite mode:

```bash
cd onyx/deployment/docker_compose
docker compose -f docker-compose.lite.yml up -d
```

For Kubernetes/Helm/Terraform there are official charts in `deployment/kubernetes/` and `deployment/helm/` — Onyx is genuinely production-ready if you want to run it for a team.

## Gotchas

- **Vespa is a memory hog.** Budget 4-8 GB just for the index container on a real corpus. The Lite stack avoids this.
- **First-time indexing is slow.** Connectors run on a schedule; kick them manually from the admin UI the first time and go make coffee.
- **Embeddings model download.** First boot pulls the sentence-transformers model — don't panic when the model server takes 3 minutes to come up.
- **Enterprise feature fences.** Some advanced features (SSO variations, SCIM, advanced RBAC, some analytics) are gated behind the Enterprise Edition. The free MIT Community Edition is still excellent.
- **LLM cost on cloud backends.** Deep Research + agentic search can make lots of LLM calls per question. Cap it with a local model or rate limits if cost is a concern.
- **Auth-by-default in dev.** Set `AUTH_TYPE=disabled` for local single-user; otherwise you're creating admin accounts every reset.

## How you could self-host it as a personal knowledge layer

The right use case for Onyx in your stack isn't "replace Claude Code" — it's **become the permanent index and chat layer over everything that isn't code**. Claude Code handles the coding loop; Onyx becomes the searchable memory of everything else.

A realistic personal setup:

1. **Run Onyx full stack on the dev box or a small home server** (16 GB RAM, Docker Compose). Put it behind Tailscale or Cloudflare Tunnel so it's reachable from anywhere without exposing ports.
2. **Connect the sources that matter:**
   - Local file connector pointed at `~/projects/` (all the project notes, markdown, guides, MEMORY.md files)
   - GitHub connector on your repos (Unicron, trading-agent-team, ai-catalogs, ai3-resources)
   - Notion / Google Drive if anything lives there
   - Gmail if you want the chat agent to search email
   - YouTube transcripts for channels you study
3. **LLM backend: Claude via API** for the chat/reasoning, **local sentence-transformers for embeddings** (free, good enough). Optionally add Gemini as a second provider for the cost sensitive Deep Research mode.
4. **Create Assistants per domain:**
   - "Trading Research" — scoped to trading-agent-team + strategy repos + crypto guides
   - "Unicron Engineer" — scoped to unicron repo + legion-command docs
   - "Design System" — scoped to ai-catalogs + frontend-design references
   - "Personal Memory" — scoped to MEMORY.md + session transcripts
5. **Point Claude Code at Onyx via MCP.** Onyx exposes an MCP server; add it to `~/.claude/settings.json` so Claude Code can query your personal knowledge base mid-coding-session. This is the real unlock: agentic RAG across your entire second brain, on tap, inside Claude Code.
6. **Schedule connector syncs** so the index stays fresh without thinking about it.

Onyx eff

title: OpenScreen — Free Open-Source Screen Studio Alternative
guide_markdown:
# OpenScreen — Free Open-Source Screen Studio Alternative

**GitHub:** https://github.com/siddharthvaddem/openscreen
**License:** MIT
**Stack:** Electron + React + TypeScript + Vite + PixiJS + Tailwind
**Platforms:** macOS 13+, Windows, Linux (PipeWire)
**Repo path:** `repos/openscreen/` (clone pending — sandbox blocked git clone in this session; run `git clone https://github.com/siddharthvaddem/openscreen.git repos/openscreen` manually)

---

## What it is

OpenScreen is a free, open-source desktop screen recorder built as a deliberate clone of [Screen Studio](https://screen.studio) — the $229 macOS app that single-handedly defined the "polished product demo with smooth auto-zoom and animated cursor" aesthetic that's now everywhere on X and YouTube. The creator's pitch is refreshingly honest: "a much simpler take, just the basics for folks who want control and don't want to pay."

That framing is accurate. OpenScreen is not trying to match Screen Studio feature-for-feature. It nails the core that makes Screen Studio recordings instantly recognizable — **automatic cursor-aware zooms**, cinematic backgrounds, motion blur, clean exports — while skipping fancier pro features. In exchange you get: free, MIT-licensed, cross-platform (Mac / Windows / Linux), and source available.

The closest analogs:
- **Screen Studio** — $229, macOS only, polished, the gold standard; OpenScreen clones its core loop
- **[Cap](https://cap.so/)** — open-source, Rust + Tauri, more feature-rich, focused on async video messaging (Loom-style)
- **Tella** — cloud-hosted SaaS, polished but subscription and not local
- **OBS Studio** — free, pro-grade, zero polish (no auto-zoom, no cursor animation)
- **QuickTime / Windows Snipping Tool** — free but bare-metal, no editing

OpenScreen sits in the "free and polished enough for 90% of demos" slot that nothing else really filled before — Cap is close but much heavier.

## How it works

OpenScreen is an Electron desktop app. The recording and editing pipeline is:

1. **Capture** — Electron's `desktopCapturer` API pulls a MediaStream for the selected screen/window. On macOS 14.2+ it requests the audio capture entitlement; on Linux it relies on PipeWire's screen capture portal. Windows has first-class system audio support.
2. **Cursor tracking** — alongside the video stream, OpenScreen records high-resolution cursor position events. This is the secret sauce: because cursor data is captured as discrete events rather than baked into the video, the editor can later generate smooth animated cursors and compute zoom targets that actually track where attention is.
3. **Editor / compositor** — a **PixiJS** scene composites the raw screen recording, a generated synthetic cursor (styled and animated), a background layer (wallpapers, colors, gradients), and effects like motion blur. PixiJS gives it hardware-accelerated 2D rendering which is why the preview is smooth.
4. **Timeline** — built on `dnd-timeline` for draggable segments, trims, and speed ramps.
5. **Auto-zoom engine** — analyzes cursor velocity and click events to place zoom keyframes automatically; you can also drop manual zooms with configurable depth and duration.
6. **Export** — renders the composed timeline out to MP4/WebM at configurable aspect ratios and resolutions.

## Core features (what actually works)

- Record a specific window or the full screen
- **Automatic zooms** driven by cursor/click events, with adjustable depth and duration
- **Manual zoom keyframes** on the timeline
- **Animated synthetic cursor** — larger, smoothed, styled separately from the OS cursor
- Microphone + system audio capture (system audio on Windows and macOS 14.2+; Linux via PipeWire)
- Background customization — wallpapers, solid colors, gradients
- Motion blur effect for smooth zoom transitions
- Annotations — text, arrows, images
- Segment trim, split, speed adjust
- Multiple aspect ratios (16:9, 9:16, 1:1, etc.) and export resolutions
- Local-first, no cloud, no account

## System requirements

- **macOS:** 13 Ventura or later; macOS 14.2+ recommended for system audio capture
- **Windows:** 10/11, works with system audio out of the box
- **Linux:** Must have PipeWire (most modern distros — Fedora, recent Ubuntu, Arch — do); X11-only systems won't work
- **RAM:** 8 GB minimum, 16 GB recommended for 4K/long recordings (Electron + PixiJS + raw frame buffers add up)
- **GPU:** Any modern integrated GPU; PixiJS uses WebGL
- **Disk:** Enough free space for raw recordings — plan ~1 GB per 5 minutes at 1440p

## Quick start

**Install from releases (recommended):**
Download from the GitHub Releases page.

macOS:
```bash
# After downloading the .dmg and dragging to Applications
xattr -rd com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Openscreen.app
open /Applications/Openscreen.app
```
(The `xattr` step is required because the app isn't notarized — Gatekeeper will otherwise refuse to launch it.)

Linux (AppImage):
```bash
chmod +x Openscreen-Linux-*.AppImage
./Openscreen-Linux-*.AppImage
```

Windows: run the installer `.exe`.

**Build from source** (for hacking or if no release matches your platform):
```bash
git clone https://github.com/siddharthvaddem/openscreen.git
cd openscreen
npm install
npm run dev        # launches Electron in dev mode with hot reload
npm run build      # produces a platform installer in dist/
```

## Gotchas

- **No notarization on macOS** — every release needs the `xattr` dequarantine step or Gatekeeper blocks it. If you share a recording workflow with non-technical people, point them at a notarized alternative instead.
- **Linux system audio is hit-or-miss.** PipeWire portal support varies by distro and desktop environment. If system audio doesn't work, fall back to capturing mic + running the app's audio through a virtual sink.
- **Electron overhead.** Startup is 1-2 seconds slower than native apps, and RAM usage sits around 400-700 MB while idle. Not ideal for older laptops.
- **Feature gap vs Screen Studio:** no multi-camera picture-in-picture, no advanced speed ramps, no per-clip color grading, no teleprompter. If those matter, stay on Screen Studio.
- **Project is young.** Expect rough edges, occasional crashes, active development. Check the issue tracker before committing to it for mission-critical recordings.

## How it compares

| Feature | OpenScreen | Screen Studio | Cap | OBS | QuickTime |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price | Free | $229 | Free / paid cloud | Free | Free |
| OSS | Yes (MIT) | No | Yes | Yes | No |
| Auto zoom | Yes | Yes (best) | Yes | No | No |
| Animated cursor | Yes | Yes (best) | Yes | No | No |
| Backgrounds/wallpapers | Yes | Yes | Yes | Manual | No |
| Motion blur | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Annotations | Yes | Yes | Limited | Plugin | No |
| Cross-platform | Mac/Win/Linux | Mac only | Mac/Win/Linux | All | Mac only |
| Polish | Good, young | Best in class | Very good | Pro but ugly | Basic |
| Cloud sharing | No | Optional | Built-in | No | No |

The honest call: if you're already paying for Screen Studio, keep using it — it's still the benchmark. If you're on Windows or Linux, or you want open-source, OpenScreen is the most direct clone of the Screen Studio aesthetic available for free. Cap is a strong alternative, especially if you want cloud sharing, but it's optimized more for async messaging than cinematic demo recording.

## What we could build with it / use it for

- **Record Unicron and trading-agent-team demos** with the same cinematic feel as Screen Studio, without the $229 tag, for X/YouTube/blog posts
- **Tutorial content** for Claude Code workflows, skill chains, AgentOps usage — the auto-zoom is exactly the style that's visually dominant on CodeTok
- **Bug repros** for open-source PRs — the animated cursor makes it obvious what you clicked; much clearer than QuickTime
- **Design review recordings** — record a web app, annotate, export in mobile aspect ratio for responsive-test showcases
- **Hack the editor** — because it's MIT + PixiJS, you can add custom effects, export presets, or AI-driven auto-zoom by forking the cursor-analysis module
- **Self-host it behind a shared drop folder** as a team's standard recording tool so everyone produces consistently styled demos
- **Feed recordings into SentrySearch** for a searchable internal demo library

## Bottom line

OpenScreen is a legitimately useful free alternative to Screen Studio for the exact style of product demo everyone is making in 2026. The feature set is narrower than Cap but more focused on the cinematic-demo aesthetic, and it works on Windows and Linux where Screen Studio does not. Worth cloning, worth having installed, worth using for any public-facing recording that doesn't justify a Screen Studio license.

title: Polymarket 99c Limit Order Arbitrage — Scalping the Resolution Tail
guide_markdown:
# Polymarket 99c Limit Order Arbitrage — Scalping the Resolution Tail

There's a specific, dumb, beautiful trade on Polymarket: post resting 99¢ bids on contracts that are almost certainly going to resolve to $1. When someone panics, needs liquidity, or fat-fingers a market sell, you eat their order at 99¢, wait a day or two, and collect $1. One cent of edge times 30-50 basis points of fee drag nets ~0.5% per cycle — but the cycles are short, the risk is well-characterized, and the capital turnover is extreme.

This is not alpha in the "predict the future" sense. It is **liquidity provision at the tail of a binary distribution**. The edge is structural.

---

## 1. What it is

Polymarket contracts are binary — they resolve to either $1 (YES wins) or $0 (NO wins). In the hours and days before resolution, many contracts have a near-certain outcome. A political contract where the result is already declared but not yet resolved. A sports contract past the final whistle. A weather contract where the day's high has already been printed. The "true" price is $1, but the order book has people selling at 98, 97, 96 for various reasons: exit-to-redeploy, position-close, loss-harvesting, or panic.

The trade: post resting limit buy orders at 99¢ (or 98, 97 laddered) and let liquidity takers hit you. When the contract resolves, you redeem for $1.

---

## 2. How it works — the mechanics

### Polymarket's order book

Polymarket runs a CLOB (Central Limit Order Book) on Polygon. Orders are signed messages held off-chain; fills settle on-chain via the Conditional Tokens Framework (CTF). Key facts:

- **Price range:** $0.01 to $0.99 (you cannot post at $1.00 exactly).
- **Tick size:** $0.01 on most markets, sometimes $0.001.
- **Fees:** scale as `min(price, 1 − price) * fee_rate`. At $0.99, your effective fee is based on 0.01 — essentially free. This is the *critical* mechanical reason the strategy is even possible.
- **Settlement:** When a market resolves YES, holders of YES tokens can redeem 1:1 for USDC. NO tokens burn. Redemption is permissionless and instant after resolution.
- **Merging:** You can also merge YES + NO tokens at any time into 1 USDC via the CTF contract, which is the other exit path.

### Why resting 99¢ bids get filled

Even on a contract "everyone knows" will resolve YES, sellers show up because:

1. **Capital rotation.** Someone with a $10k position wants to redeploy before resolution rather than wait two days — they'll take 99¢ to move on.
2. **Tax harvesting.** Realizing a gain at 99¢ vs waiting for $1 has cleaner bookkeeping.
3. **Panic / FUD.** Rumors of oracle disputes, delays, or manipulation. Occasionally right, usually wrong.
4. **Fat fingers.** Market sells by people who meant to market buy, or by scripts with broken sign logic.
5. **Resolution risk tail.** Actual non-zero probability of a dispute or adverse resolution. *This is the one real risk you are being paid for.*

### The math

Round-trip PnL on a single fill:

```
PnL = (payout − entry) − fees
    = ($1.00 − $0.99) − (2 × fee_rate × $0.01)   [fees on both sides capped by min(p, 1−p)]
    ≈ $0.01 − $0.0002
    ≈ $0.0098 per share ≈ 0.99% gross return
```

But capital turnover is high. If you cycle every 24 hours, that's ~250% annualized simple, compounded. With laddering (bids at 97, 98, 99) you catch more fills at higher gross margin:

- 97¢ fill → 3¢ gross, ~2.9¢ net → ~3% return
- 98¢ fill → 2¢ gross, ~1.9¢ net → ~1.9% return
- 99¢ fill → 1¢ gross, ~0.98¢ net → ~1% return

Expected weighted return per capital deployed depends entirely on fill distribution, which depends entirely on what kind of "almost-certain" contracts you target.

---

## 3. Key mechanics — what to target

Not every contract is tradeable this way. The sweet spot:

- **Resolution within 24-72 hours.** Longer holds compress annualized return and expose you to more disputes.
- **Clean resolution source.** Weather station data, election commission, sports final score. Avoid interpretation-heavy markets ("Will X tweet about Y") — those are where disputes happen.
- **Liquid enough to fill.** You need at least a few dozen USDC of daily volume at the 95-99 range for the strategy to be worth running.
- **Post-certainty window.** The actual outcome is known but resolution hasn't executed. For elections, this is the 48-72 hours between "AP calls it" and "Polymarket oracle confirms." For sports, it's the 1-24 hours after the game. For weather, it's the post-midnight period after the daily high is recorded.
- **Avoid any market with oracle controversy.** Check Discord, Twitter, and the market's dispute history.

---

## 4. Automation — how to replicate

The Polymarket CLOB has a Python client (`py-clob-client`) and a REST/WebSocket API. Full automation takes maybe 300 lines of Python.

### Minimum viable bot

```python
from py_clob_client.client import ClobClient
from py_clob_client.clob_types import OrderArgs, OrderType

client = ClobClient(host="https://clob.polymarket.com", key=PRIVATE_KEY, chain_id=137)
client.set_api_creds(client.create_or_derive_api_creds())

# 1. Scan all markets with end_date within 72h
markets = client.get_markets()
targets = [m for m in markets if is_near_resolution(m) and is_clean_source(m)]

# 2. For each target's YES token, post a laddered bid
for m in targets:
    token_id = m["tokens"][0]["token_id"]  # YES
    for price, size in [(0.99, 100), (0.98, 50), (0.97, 25)]:
        order = client.create_order(OrderArgs(
            price=price, size=size, side="BUY",
            token_id=token_id
        ))
        client.post_order(order, OrderType.GTC)

# 3. Watch fills via WS, redeem after resolution
```

### Sizing and risk

- **Cap per market.** Never more than ~2% of capital in any single market. Oracle disputes are the tail risk and they hit a single market at a time.
- **Diversify across 20-50 concurrent markets.** This is the whole point — aggregate the tail so a single bad resolution doesn't blow up the strategy.
- **Hard stop on dispute signals.** Monitor UMA (Polymarket's oracle) dispute status. If a market enters dispute, cancel orders immediately and consider merging YES/NO to exit.
- **Time-based cancel.** If a bid hasn't filled within its expected window, cancel and rotate capital.

### Existing tools

- **`direkturcrypto/polymarket-terminal`** — public repo for copy/scalp/sniper on Polymarket. Not exactly this strategy but the CLOB plumbing is reusable.
- **`py-clob-client`** — official Polymarket Python client. The only dependency you actually need.

---

## 5. Risks — the honest list

1. **Oracle disputes.** UMA can rule against the "obvious" outcome. Rare but has happened (contested election calls, ambiguous sports outcomes). This is the *real* risk you're being paid 1¢ for. If UMA rules NO on a contract where you bought YES at 99¢, you lose ~$0.99 per share. One bad resolution can erase months of edge. **Mitigation: diversification + hard dispute filter + never touch contested markets.**
2. **Smart contract risk.** CTF contract bugs, Polygon bridge issues, Polymarket operator actions.
3. **Resolution delays.** Your capital sits longer than modeled, compressing annualized return. Not catastrophic, just disappointing.
4. **Front-running / adverse selection.** The 1¢ of panic sellers knows something you don't about 5% of the time. That's priced in.
5. **Regulatory.** US persons technically can't trade Polymarket. This is your call, not mine to advise on.
6. **Competition from other bots.** This strategy is known. Depth at 99¢ has thinned as more bots run it. You need to be either faster, or post at 97-98¢ and accept more fill variance.

---

## 6. How this plugs into your trading-agent-team

This is a **capital-efficient, low-touch, low-correlation strategy** that fits the Unicron multi-strategy arena model well. It doesn't compete with the fast-cycler or Oracle Commander — it runs in parallel on Polymarket collateral while the perp strategies run on Hyperliquid collateral.

**Concrete integration ideas:**

1. **Pure-rules execution, zero AI in the hot path** — matches your rule from `feedback_rules_vs_agents.md`. The selection logic ("clean source, <72h to resolution, not disputed") is 100% deterministic. No LLM, no ML. The AI layer only runs at market-discovery time: nightly, an agent scans new markets and classifies them as eligible / not eligible with reasoning. Humans review the classification before markets go live.

2. **Watchdog pattern is a perfect fit.** Unicron's oversight spec already has a watchdog layer. For this strategy, the watchdog monitors UMA dispute events per open market. Dispute detected → cancel + exit via YES/NO merge immediately. This is the highest-leverage line of code in the whole bot.

3. **Challenge-game sweep.** Parameters: bid ladder shape `[97, 98, 99]` weights, per-market cap, time-to-resolution threshold, source-cleanliness score. Fitness: Sharpe of simulated PnL on replayed Polymarket historical data (available via

title: Polymarket Weather Trading — Ensemble Forecasts as Edge
guide_markdown:
# Polymarket Weather Trading — Ensemble Forecasts as Edge

One of the most-repeated Polymarket folk stories of 2025 is "a student built a six-figure portfolio trading weather contracts from his dorm with a DIY sensor rig." The sensor-rig version of the story is mostly myth — the actual edge is more boring, more reproducible, and more interesting: **multi-model ensemble forecasting against a retail-priced order book**. The weather station is optional flavor. The ensemble is the alpha.

This guide covers the strategy, the real infrastructure the top traders use, why *weather* was the perfect market to build this on, and what's replicable.

---

## 1. What it is

Polymarket runs hundreds of daily/weekly weather contracts: "High temperature in NYC on March 15 between 42°F and 45°F," "Will it rain tomorrow in London," "Max temp in Buenos Aires above X." Each bucketed range is a separate binary contract. Dozens of top wallets have made $20k–$2M+ trading these markets, and several of the top 10 Polymarket wallets by PnL are weather-only.

Named traders:

- **gopfan2** — $2M+ net, almost entirely from weather. Known for simple price rules (buy YES under $0.15, buy NO over $0.45, ~$1 max risk per position) and extreme volume.
- **neobrother** — $20k+ from "temperature laddering" — buying low-cost bets across many temperature buckets to cover a wider range than the market implied.
- **Hans323** — $1.11M on a single $92k bet on London's weather (~8% implied probability).

The edge isn't knowing the weather better than NOAA. The edge is **knowing it better than the order book**, which is a much lower bar.

---

## 2. How it works — the actual strategy

### Core thesis

Weather forecasts from professional models (GFS, ECMWF, UKMO, NWS, ICON, GEM, HRRR) are *extremely* good 12-72 hours out. Trained 4-model ensembles hit ~70-75% accuracy on daily-high temperature buckets and daily precipitation. Polymarket contracts on those same events trade on retail sentiment, copy trading, and stale prices — often for hours after a new model run has materially shifted the forecast.

That gap is the edge. You're arbitraging retail prediction market prices against publicly available, free, scientifically rigorous physical models.

### The ensemble

No single model is reliable. The top bot (WeatherBot) uses a 4-model ensemble weighted as:

| Model | Weight |
|-------|--------|
| ECMWF (European) | 35% |
| GFS (US global) | 25% |
| UKMO (UK Met Office) | 20% |
| NWS (US, bias-corrected MOS) | 20% |

With outlier penalization — if one model disagrees sharply, its weight gets cut. Degen Doppler runs a much larger 13-model ensemble (Tomorrow.io, Pirate, Visual Crossing, etc.) and dynamically reweights by recent accuracy per region and time-of-day.

For each Polymarket bucket `[T_lo, T_hi]` on day D, you compute:

```
P_ensemble(T_lo ≤ T_actual ≤ T_hi) = Σ_m w_m · P_m(T_lo ≤ T ≤ T_hi)
```

where `P_m` is derived from the ensemble-member spread (or from raw ensemble members in the case of GFS's 31-member GEFS).

### The trade

- If `P_ensemble > ask_price + edge_threshold` → buy YES.
- If `P_ensemble < bid_price − edge_threshold` → buy NO (equivalent to selling YES).
- Size with Kelly or fractional Kelly on `P_ensemble` vs market price.
- Exit either at resolution or when price converges to fair value (rolling the capital to the next mispricing).

### Why this works

1. **Polymarket weather markets are liquid but not efficient.** There's enough volume to trade, but retail traders drive prices with gut feel, not NWS MOS output.
2. **Model runs update every 6 hours.** When GFS 12z drops and shows NYC 5°F warmer than the 06z run, the probability stack for the daily high buckets shifts instantly. Polymarket lags this by 30-90 minutes. That lag is a free option.
3. **Bucketed contracts enable laddering.** Instead of one bet, you buy a probability-weighted basket across 3-5 adjacent buckets around the ensemble mode, which dramatically reduces variance.
4. **Weather is a mean-reverting, well-understood physical process.** Unlike political or sports markets, there are no hidden catalysts, no insider info, no interpretation risk.

---

## 3. Key mechanics

**Data sources (all free):**
- NOAA NOMADS — GFS grib2 files, refreshed 4x/day
- ECMWF Open Data — since Jan 2022, free up to 10 days out
- UKMO & ICON via open APIs
- NWS API for MOS station forecasts (this is the one closest to Polymarket's resolution source)
- Visual Crossing, Open-Meteo — aggregated APIs if you don't want to parse grib2

**Resolution source matters.** Polymarket weather markets resolve against specific weather station reports (usually the "official" NWS observation for the city). Your model needs to predict *that station*, not the city average. This is where NWS MOS (station-specific bias-corrected output) dominates raw GFS.

**Position lifecycle:**
1. Pull new model runs every 6 hours (00z, 06z, 12z, 18z UTC).
2. Recompute ensemble PDF for each open market's resolution variable.
3. Diff against current Polymarket CLOB best-bid/best-ask.
4. Size positions with Kelly or fixed fraction. Most successful bots cap per-position risk at $1-$100.
5. Post limit orders (not market orders — slippage kills the edge on thin markets).
6. On the next model run, recompute and either scale up, reverse, or hold.

**Fee structure quirk:** Polymarket fees scale by `min(price, 1−price)`, so extreme-price contracts (near $0.01 or $0.99) have the lowest effective fees. This is also what enables the 99c limit arbitrage strategy (see `polymarket-99c-limit-arbitrage.md`).

---

## 4. The infrastructure — what's actually running

Three public references exist:

### `suislanchez/polymarket-kalshi-weather-bot`
Full-stack reference implementation. Trades both Kalshi (KXHIGH series) and Polymarket. Uses **GFS 31-member ensemble** (GEFS) forecasts plus — notably — BTC 5-minute microstructure as an auxiliary signal. Kelly sizing, signal calibration, React dashboard. Claimed max profit ~$1.8k. Best starting point for a working codebase.

### `hcharper/polyBot-Weather`
Simpler single-model bot. Educational.

### WeatherBot (weatherbot.finance) & Degen Doppler
Commercial tools. Closed source. WeatherBot publishes its 4-model weighting scheme as marketing; Degen Doppler publishes its 13-model list. You can replicate both from public APIs.

### The "dorm / weather station" angle
The viral story about a student using a rooftop weather station for edge doesn't hold up: a single-point sensor can't beat a continental-scale numerical weather model for even 12-hour forecasts, because the model already ingests tens of thousands of station observations. Where a *local* sensor helps is **arbitraging the last-hour resolution print** — detecting whether the NWS station has already recorded the high for the day, which Polymarket prices don't always reflect until it's official. That's a nowcasting edge, not a forecasting edge, and it requires co-location near (or API access to) the specific resolution station. Short range, narrow edge, real but overstated.

---

## 5. How to replicate

**Minimal viable weather trader (1 weekend):**

```bash
pip install polymarket-py open-meteo-requests requests numpy
```

1. Use Open-Meteo's free ensemble API (GFS + ECMWF + ICON + GEM) — skip grib2 parsing entirely. Returns raw ensemble members.
2. Pull current Polymarket weather markets via the CLOB REST API.
3. For each market, compute `P_ensemble(bucket)` as the fraction of ensemble members falling in the bucket.
4. Buy any bucket where `P_ensemble − ask > 0.10` with $1-10 per position.
5. Hold to resolution.

This is enough to learn the edge. Scaling to $10k+ requires real-time order management, slippage control, and a watchdog that can cut positions on model disagreement.

**Data path to productionize:**
- Open-Meteo → GFS/ECMWF/ICON ensemble members
- NWS API → station MOS forecasts
- NOAA NOMADS → raw GEFS 31-member if you want more resolution
- ECMWF Open Data → raw IFS ensemble (2 runs/day free, 4 runs paid)
- Ensemble reweighting by recent hit-rate per city/season

---

## 6. How this plugs into your trading-agent-team

The trading-agent-team is built around crypto perps. Polymarket weather is an **uncorrelated PnL source** — not a single tick of correlation with BTC, HYPE, or anything in the existing portfolio. That alone is worth a subproject, especially for Unicron which is meant to be a multi-strategy platform.

**Concrete integration ideas:**

1. **New "environmental" arena in Unicron.** Add a Polymarket connector alongside the Hyperliquid one. Run a weather ensemble bot as a sub-strategy. Its PnL curve will be orthogonal to the crypto strategies, which smooths the aggregate Sharpe.

2. **Pure-rules execution, AI-only for ensemble weighting.** Per your rule (feedback_rules_vs_agents.md: pure rules for trade execution, AI only for the research/optimization layer), the weather bot is an ideal fit. Rules: "if `P_ensemble > ask + 10pp`, buy." AI layer: nigh

title: primer.md — The Living Handoff Document Pattern
guide_markdown:
# primer.md — The Living Handoff Document Pattern

**Attributed to:** @keshavsuki (on X/Twitter), though the broader "living handoff document" lineage predates the specific `primer.md` naming — Yusuke Kamiyamane (@ykdojo) popularized a similar `HANDOFF.md` pattern, and various `SESSION.md` / `STATE.md` / `CONTEXT.md` variants circulate in the awesome-claude-code ecosystem. The `primer.md` naming and the specific "Claude rewrites it at session end" mechanic are the contribution being catalogued here.

> **Research note:** The specific @keshavsuki post was not directly recoverable through web search at the time of writing. The pattern described below is reconstructed from the broader family of handoff-document patterns it belongs to, cross-referenced with the Claude Code hook system that makes the "auto-rewrite on session end" mechanic possible. Treat specific code snippets below as reference implementations, not verbatim copies of keshavsuki's original.

## What it is

`primer.md` is a **sibling file to `CLAUDE.md`** that serves a fundamentally different purpose:

- **CLAUDE.md** = permanent project knowledge (conventions, stack, behavioral rules). Rarely changes.
- **primer.md** = live project *state* (what's happening right now, what's blocked, what's next). Rewritten every session.

The core mechanic: at the end of every Claude Code session, Claude rewrites `primer.md` with a snapshot of where the project currently stands and what the next session should do first. At the start of every session, Claude reads `primer.md` (via a CLAUDE.md pointer or via the `additionalDirectories` hook) and resumes exactly where the previous session left off — no "what were we doing again" dance, no re-reading five files to rebuild context.

It is a **living handoff document** between Claude and its future self.

## Why this pattern exists

Claude Code has no memory across sessions. Every new session starts cold. The options for rebuilding context are:

1. **Re-explain to Claude manually** — slow, lossy, requires *you* to remember.
2. **Rely on CLAUDE.md** — it holds permanent rules but not current state ("we just finished phase 2, phase 3 is blocked on the Redis migration").
3. **Use `/resume`** — works within a single conversation thread but not across branch-switches, compactions, or new terminals.
4. **Ask Claude to write a handoff document before starting fresh** — the @ykdojo pattern. Works, but requires you to remember to ask.
5. **Make the handoff document self-maintaining** — the primer.md pattern. The hook handles it automatically.

`primer.md` is option 5, and its value is that it removes the human from the loop. You never have to remember to update it.

## How it works under the hood

The pattern has three parts:

### 1. The file itself — structured session state

```markdown
# Project Primer
_Last updated: 2026-04-08 14:32 UTC (session ended)_

## Current status
Phase 3 of the trading-agent-team integration. Arena wire-up is COMPLETE
and green. Legion port is IN PROGRESS — we're 60% through migrating the
Command tab from /finance into /unicron/command.

## What changed this session
- Ported ARSENAL tab component + its three sub-widgets (bot cards, metric
  rows, status dots). Tests green.
- Discovered: the old Legion Command chart code depends on Plotly 5.x;
  /unicron is on Plotly 6.x. Needs shim or upgrade.
- Added your CSS vars to `src/styles/legion-theme.css`.

## Next up (start here)
1. Resolve the Plotly version mismatch — decide: shim or upgrade all of unicron.
   Relevant files: `src/charts/LegionChart.tsx`, `package.json` (line 42).
2. Finish migrating RANKINGS tab (parallel structure to ARSENAL — should
   be ~30 min if Plotly is resolved).
3. Run full visual-regression suite before declaring Phase 3 done.

## Blockers
- Plotly version decision (above). Needs your input if we go the
  upgrade route since it touches other tabs.

## Open questions
- Does the old `session_state` singleton in `legion_command.py` need to
  survive the port, or can we replace it with Zustand like the rest of
  unicron?

## Don't forget
- The `.env` in `/unicron` has a placeholder HL_PRIVATE_KEY — you
  need to set this before running live.
- Arena's WebSocket reconnect logic is the reference implementation for
  any new real-time wiring.
```

**Key sections:**
- **Current status** — one paragraph, no more. Where is the project *right now*?
- **What changed this session** — delta from last primer. Keeps momentum visible.
- **Next up** — explicit ordered list. First item should be *immediately actionable* by a fresh Claude with zero other context.
- **Blockers** — things that need human input or external resolution.
- **Open questions** — uncertainties worth surfacing before the next session dives in.
- **Don't forget** — sharp edges, gotchas, state that lives outside the code (env vars, external services, half-applied migrations).

### 2. The CLAUDE.md anchor — tell Claude the file exists

Add this to your project `CLAUDE.md`:

```markdown
## Session continuity
- At the **start** of every session: read `primer.md` first. It contains
  the current project state and next steps from the previous session.
- Follow the "Next up" list unless the user redirects.
- At the **end** of every session: rewrite `primer.md` from scratch.
  Do not append — the file is a snapshot, not a log.
- Structure: Current status / What changed / Next up / Blockers / Open
  questions / Don't forget.
- Keep it under 150 lines. If it's growing, something is wrong — the
  project has either stalled or needs a real retro.
```

### 3. The hook — automate the rewrite

Claude Code hooks (configured in `.claude/settings.json`) can run arbitrary commands on lifecycle events. The relevant one here is the **Stop hook** — fires when a session ends (user exits, or agent finishes its final turn).

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "claude -p 'Rewrite primer.md to reflect the current project state. Use the structure defined in CLAUDE.md under Session continuity. Do not append — replace the file entirely. Be specific about what the next session should do first.' --allowedTools Read,Write,Glob,Grep"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**How this works:**
- Session ends → Stop hook fires.
- The hook spawns a fresh `claude -p` (non-interactive) subprocess.
- That subprocess reads the current transcript context (via the `CLAUDE_TRANSCRIPT_PATH` env var the hook provides), analyzes what happened, and writes a new `primer.md`.
- The subprocess is restricted to `Read,Write,Glob,Grep` — it can't accidentally run tests, commit, or touch anything else.
- Next session starts → reads `primer.md` per the CLAUDE.md instruction → resumes cleanly.

**Alternative: PreCompact hook.** If your sessions are long and you rely on compaction rather than explicit exits, use the `PreCompact` hook instead. Same logic, fires before Claude Code compresses context rather than when the session terminates.

**Alternative: manual command.** If you don't want automation, add a slash command:

```markdown
# .claude/commands/prime.md
Rewrite primer.md with the current project state per the structure in
CLAUDE.md. Then summarize what you wrote in 2 sentences.
```

Now `/prime` at the end of any session does the same thing without a hook.

## Key mechanics

**What makes primer.md different from HANDOFF.md / SESSION.md / a changelog:**

1. **Snapshot, not log.** It is *rewritten*, not appended to. This is critical — a log grows unboundedly and loses the "what matters now" signal. A snapshot stays focused.
2. **Self-maintaining via hook.** The human never types it. This is what keshavsuki's contribution adds over the manual handoff pattern.
3. **Action-oriented "Next up."** The first line of the first next-up item should be *immediately executable*. No "continue working on the thing" — specific file, specific change.
4. **Paired with CLAUDE.md, not replacing it.** CLAUDE.md is permanent rules; primer.md is state. Don't conflate them.

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. Create the file with a starter template
cd my-project
cat > primer.md <<'EOF'
# Project Primer
_Last updated: [session init]_

## Current status
Project just bootstrapped. No work yet.

## Next up
1. Define what we're actually building.
EOF

# 2. Add the CLAUDE.md anchor
# (paste the "Session continuity" block above into CLAUDE.md)

# 3. Configure the Stop hook
# Edit .claude/settings.json and paste the hook JSON above

# 4. Start a session, do some work, exit
claude
> (work happens)
> exit

# 5. Verify primer.md was rewritten
cat primer.md
```

If the hook didn't fire, check `claude --debug` output and `.claude/settings.json` syntax — hooks silently skip on JSON errors.

## Cross-reference: how this complements your MEMORY.md system

you already run a related but distinct pattern at `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md` — an index o

title: Quant Project Ideas — 15 Projects Worth Building
guide_markdown:
# Quant Project Ideas — 15 Projects Worth Building

A curated, opinionated list of quant projects — skewed toward the ones that actually teach you something and give you a tool you'll keep using. The seed for this list is a Twitter thread credited to @heidioftheeast with ideas like probability of backtest overfitting, Bayesian Black-Litterman, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, and Kalman filters. I have expanded it with adjacent projects that round out a real quant portfolio, and ranked by build-value (difficulty × payoff × reusability across future work).

Each entry: **what it is → the math in one line → a canonical repo → difficulty → why build it → how it slots into your stack**.

Difficulty scale: 🟢 weekend · 🟡 1-2 weeks · 🟠 1 month · 🔴 multi-month

---

## Tier 1 — Must-build infrastructure

These aren't strategies; they're the *scaffolding* every quant portfolio needs. Build them first, use them forever.

### 1. Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) 🟡

**What:** Lopez de Prado / Bailey / Borwein's framework for estimating how much of a backtested Sharpe is spurious. Uses Combinatorially Symmetric Cross-Validation (CSCV) to compute PBO, performance degradation, and related statistics (Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio, Minimum Track Record Length, Deflated Sharpe Ratio).

**Math:** Split your N-column return matrix of `N` strategy variants into `S` submatrices, enumerate all `C(S, S/2)` train/test splits, and compute the fraction of splits where the in-sample-best strategy underperforms median out-of-sample. That fraction is PBO.

**Repo:** [`esvhd/pypbo`](https://github.com/esvhd/pypbo) — reference Python implementation with PBO, PSR, MinTRL, DSR.

**Difficulty:** 🟡 1-2 weeks to understand and integrate.

**Why build it:** Because every backtest you'll ever run is at risk of being overfit and you currently have no number for how much. The difference between a strategy with PBO=0.10 and PBO=0.60 is the difference between "ship it" and "throw it out" — and without this you are guessing.

**Plugs into your stack:** Direct gate for the challenge-game tournament flow. Any ensemble that emerges from `/challenge-game` should pass a PBO check before promotion to paper-trading. Specifically the Phase 12 Oracle Commander finding (rolodex WR overfit) is the exact failure mode PBO detects. This is arguably the single highest-leverage tool on this whole list for you.

---

### 2. Walk-Forward + Purged K-Fold CV Harness 🟡

**What:** Cross-validation that respects time ordering and purges look-ahead leakage. Lopez de Prado's Purged K-Fold leaves a gap between train and test to prevent label leakage from overlapping samples.

**Math:** Standard K-fold but with an embargo: if sample `i` is in the test set and sample `j` in train shares any information window with `i`, drop `j`. Purging removes samples whose labels span the test period.

**Repo:** [`hudson-and-thames/mlfinlab`](https://github.com/hudson-and-thames/mlfinlab) — implements Purged K-Fold, Combinatorial Purged CV, and the rest of *Advances in Financial Machine Learning*.

**Difficulty:** 🟡 1-2 weeks.

**Why build it:** Regular sklearn cross-validation is subtly wrong for financial data. Purged K-Fold fixes it.

**Plugs into your stack:** Pair with PBO in the challenge-game validation gate. Use for all ML-layer training in Oracle Commander / Rolodex.

---

### 3. Research Infrastructure: bar sampling, labeling, feature engineering 🟠

**What:** Dollar bars instead of time bars, triple-barrier labeling, fractional differentiation for stationarity without losing memory. All from the first chapters of *Advances in Financial Machine Learning*.

**Math:** Dollar bars sample whenever cumulative traded dollar volume crosses a threshold (better sampling distribution than time bars). Triple-barrier labels each observation as +1/-1/0 depending on which horizon / SL / TP barrier hits first. Fractional differentiation: `(1 − L)^d` with non-integer `d` preserves long memory while achieving stationarity.

**Repo:** [`hudson-and-thames/mlfinlab`](https://github.com/hudson-and-thames/mlfinlab) (same).

**Difficulty:** 🟠 1 month to absorb end-to-end.

**Why build it:** Time-bar OHLCV is what every retail trader uses and every professional abandoned a decade ago. The research gap is real.

**Plugs into your stack:** Rebuild the trading-agent-team feature pipeline on dollar bars — the fast-cycler and graduated-TP strategies will almost certainly look different (and probably better) when fed cleaner inputs.

---

## Tier 2 — Classical quant strategies with real math

### 4. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Pairs Trading 🟡

**What:** Fit an OU mean-reverting process to the spread between two cointegrated assets. Trade the spread when it deviates from its long-run mean. The classic stat-arb setup.

**Math:** OU process `dX_t = θ(μ − X_t) dt + σ dW_t`. Fit `θ, μ, σ` via maximum likelihood on the discretized residuals of a cointegrating regression `Y = α + β X + ε`. Trade when `|residual − μ| > k · σ`, exit at mean. Half-life of mean reversion is `ln(2) / θ`.

**Repo:** [`david-alber/Pairs-Trading-as-application-to-the-Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Process`](https://github.com/david-alber/Pairs-Trading-as-application-to-the-Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Process) and [`cantaro86/Financial-Models-Numerical-Methods`](https://github.com/cantaro86/Financial-Models-Numerical-Methods) (the OU notebook is particularly clean).

**Difficulty:** 🟡 1-2 weeks.

**Why build it:** It's the canonical example for learning how to turn a stochastic differential equation into a trading rule. After you've done it once, half the academic literature opens up.

**Plugs into your stack:** Crypto pairs (e.g., ETH/BTC perp spread, or HYPE/SOL correlation) are great OU candidates on Hyperliquid. Add as a new sub-strategy — uncorrelated with the directional fast-cyclers.

---

### 5. Kalman Filter Dynamic Hedge Ratio 🟡

**What:** Instead of fitting a *fixed* cointegration coefficient `β` from OLS, let `β` drift over time via a Kalman filter. Adapts pairs-trading to regime changes.

**Math:** State-space model where `β_t` is the latent state with a random walk prior, observation equation `y_t = β_t x_t + ε_t`. Standard Kalman update gives a time-varying posterior mean of `β_t` that adapts on every new observation.

**Repo:** [`msekatchev/kalman-filter-asset-prices`](https://github.com/msekatchev/kalman-filter-asset-prices) and [`QuantConnect/Research` Kalman Filter Based Pairs Trading notebook](https://github.com/QuantConnect/Research/blob/master/Analysis/02%20Kalman%20Filter%20Based%20Pairs%20Trading.ipynb).

**Difficulty:** 🟡 1-2 weeks.

**Why build it:** Kalman filters are one of the few pieces of math every practitioner uses and every textbook explains badly. Pairs trading is the clearest use case to actually grok them.

**Plugs into your stack:** Generalizes OU pairs from #4. Also useful as a *smoother* for any noisy signal — rolling Hawkes branching ratio, funding rate imbalance, OI momentum. The filter is a reusable primitive beyond pairs trading.

---

### 6. Bayesian Black-Litterman Portfolio Allocation 🟠

**What:** Black-Litterman blends market-implied equilibrium returns with the investor's subjective views into a posterior distribution of expected returns. The "Bayesian" version treats it properly as a conjugate-normal Bayesian update instead of the classical BL closed form, letting you express non-Gaussian views and uncertainty.

**Math:** Prior: `π ~ N(Π, τ Σ)` where `Π` is reverse-optimized from market weights. Views: `P μ = Q + ε, ε ~ N(0, Ω)`. Posterior: `μ | views ~ N(μ̂, Σ̂)` with

```
μ̂ = [(τΣ)⁻¹ + P' Ω⁻¹ P]⁻¹ [(τΣ)⁻¹ Π + P' Ω⁻¹ Q]
```

PyMC version lets you specify full posteriors on views.

**Repos:**
- Classical closed-form: [`robertmartin8/PyPortfolioOpt`](https://github.com/robertmartin8/PyPortfolioOpt) (cookbook notebook `4-Black-Litterman-Allocation.ipynb`)
- QuantEcon Bayesian notebook: [`quantecon-notebooks-python/black_litterman.ipynb`](https://github.com/QuantEcon/quantecon-notebooks-python/blob/master/black_litterman.ipynb)
- PyMC general: [`pymc-devs/pymc`](https://github.com/pymc-devs/pymc)

**Difficulty:** 🟠 1 month if you're doing the full Bayesian version in PyMC.

**Why build it:** It's the canonical way to combine a strategy's signal ("I think BTC has +5% expected return next week") with market-neutral portfolio math. Most retail approaches ignore covariance entirely; this teaches you to respect it.

**Plugs into your stack:** Position-sizing layer for the multi-coin trading-agent-team. Current approach is mostly equal-weight across 8 coins — BL would let each sub-strategy express its own "view" on a coin's expected return and the portfolio optimizer would blend them with the correlation matrix. Cleanest upgrade path to proper risk-parity allocation.

---

### 7. Deflated Sharpe Ratio + Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio 🟢

**What:** Already partially covered in #1 via pypbo, but worth doing as a standalone. PSR tells you the probability that an observe

title: World Labs — Marble and the Era of Generative 3D Worlds
guide_markdown:
# World Labs — Marble and the Era of Generative 3D Worlds

**Company:** World Labs (https://www.worldlabs.ai)
**Founders:** Fei-Fei Li (Stanford, ImageNet, "AI godmother"), Justin Johnson, Ben Mildenhall (co-inventor of NeRF), Christoph Lassner
**Product:** **Marble** — a commercial 3D world generation model (launched Nov 2025)
**Status:** Closed-source commercial product. Web app in beta, no open weights, no public API at launch. Access is via waitlist → browser UI.
**Repo:** None — not open source. Nothing to clone.

---

## What it is

World Labs is Fei-Fei Li's "spatial intelligence" startup. Their thesis, stated plainly by Li, is that the next leap in AI is not bigger language models but systems that understand and generate **3D space** — because physical reality, robotics, AR/VR, creative tools, and scientific simulation all live in 3D, not in flat text or 2D pixels. She calls the category **Large World Models (LWMs)**, positioned as the 3D-native cousin of LLMs.

**Marble**, launched in November 2025, is their first commercial product and the first public instance of an LWM you can actually poke. Feed it a text description, one or more images, a video clip, or a rough blocky 3D layout, and it generates a complete, explorable, **persistent** 3D environment — a room, a landscape, a whole stylized scene. You can then fly a camera through it, edit it with AI-native tools, or export it as Gaussian splats, meshes, or rendered video.

This is fundamentally a different product from Hunyuan3D-2 or Tripo (see `guides/hunyuan3d-2.md` and `guides/blender-mcp-tripo-pipeline.md`). Those tools generate **single objects** — a chair, a character, a prop. Marble generates **environments** — the whole tea room, including the walls, the lighting, the objects, and the geometric relationships between them. It's a generator at the scale of Unreal Engine levels, not individual assets.

---

## How it works (what we can infer)

World Labs has not published full technical papers, but they've been surprisingly open about the high-level architecture in interviews and case studies. The approach is a hybrid that borrows from several active research threads:

**1. 3D Gaussian Splatting for appearance.** Marble represents the visual content of a scene as a dense cloud of 3D Gaussians — each an anisotropic blob with position, scale, orientation, color, and opacity. This is the same technique that replaced NeRFs as the leading photorealistic 3D representation in 2023–2024, pioneered partly by co-founder Ben Mildenhall's lab work. Gaussians are cheap to render (real-time rasterization, not volumetric ray marching) and give extremely high fidelity for static scenes.

**2. "Collider mesh" for geometry.** Alongside the Gaussians, Marble generates a low-poly triangle mesh that defines the physical boundaries of the space. This is the bit that makes the scene usable, not just lookable — the mesh is what a camera collides with, what an avatar walks on, what a physics engine simulates against. It also anchors the Gaussians so they don't drift or blur when edited.

**3. Discrete spatial state, not frame prediction.** This is the key claim that separates Marble from video-model competitors like Sora, Veo, and Runway. Those models predict "what pixel comes next" — you move the camera, they roll the generative dice, and the world changes subtly each time you look away. Marble generates **one** scene up front and keeps it fixed: move the camera away from a chair and back, the chair is in exactly the same place, with exactly the same lighting on exactly the same surface. This is table stakes for a usable creative tool and impossible for a pure video model without explicit memory.

**4. Multi-modal conditioning.** Text prompts, images, videos, and coarse 3D layouts can all condition the generation. The 3D layout path is the interesting one — you sketch a blocky arrangement ("couch here, table here, window there") and Marble fills in the visual details while respecting your structure. World Labs calls this a **hybrid 3D editor**: block out the geometry you care about, let the model hallucinate the rest.

The underlying generative model is almost certainly a diffusion transformer operating on a 3D latent representation (probably a voxel or triplane latent) that decodes to the Gaussian + mesh pair. They haven't confirmed the architecture publicly. Training data is rumored to be a mix of photogrammetric scans, synthetic UE5/Unity scenes, and multiview image collections — standard LWM training fare.

---

## How it compares to the rest of the world-generation landscape

This is a crowded research area as of 2026. Here's where Marble sits:

**vs. Google DeepMind Genie 3 (2025):** Genie 3 is an *interactive* world model — you press keys and it generates the next frame like a video game being dreamt in real time. Impressive, but it suffers from the exact problem Marble avoids: it has limited persistence, the world drifts, and you can't export anything. Genie is a research demo of interactive video; Marble is a product that outputs files.

**vs. NVIDIA GET3D / Magic3D / Scenescape (2023):** Earlier generations of scene generators. Scenescape in particular pioneered "generate a mesh you can fly through from a single image" but at much lower quality and with visible tiling artifacts. Marble is a clean generational leap.

**vs. Luma Dream Machine + Genie-style approaches:** Luma focuses on video and NeRF-from-video capture, not outright world generation. Different problem.

**vs. Hunyuan3D-2 / Tripo (single-object generators):** Completely different scope. Hunyuan3D-2 makes a chair. Marble makes the room the chair is in. You'd use them together — Marble for the environment, Hunyuan3D-2/Tripo for hero assets you want more control over.

**vs. Meta's "world models" work (Yann LeCun's V-JEPA line):** Meta is pursuing world models as **prediction** systems for robotics and planning — not renderable, not creative tools. Different audience entirely.

**vs. Wayve / 1X / Tesla world models:** These are driving / robotics world models, tuned for dynamics prediction, not aesthetic scene generation. Adjacent but separate category.

Marble is, as of early 2026, the **only product** that combines generation quality, persistence, editing, and standard export formats. That's why it matters.

## System requirements

None. Marble runs entirely in World Labs' cloud. You use it through a web app in a modern browser. No GPU required, no install, no setup. That's the upside of a closed commercial product.

The downsides:
- **Waitlist access** at launch; not everyone gets in immediately.
- **No self-hosting, no private data.** Everything you generate is on their servers.
- **No open weights.** You can't fine-tune it, you can't distill it, you can't run it offline. If World Labs shuts down or hikes prices, you have no fallback.
- **Pricing is credit-based**, similar to Midjourney/Runway. Expect to pay for serious use.
- **Export quality** is good but not infinite — the exported Gaussian splats and meshes carry artifacts typical of both representations.

## Quick start

There's nothing to install. The workflow is:

1. Sign up at https://www.worldlabs.ai and join the waitlist (or use an invite)
2. Log into the Marble web app
3. Pick an input modality:
   - **Text:** "a cyberpunk alleyway at night, neon signs, wet pavement, dense fog"
   - **Image:** upload a reference photo
   - **Video:** upload a short clip
   - **3D layout:** block out geometry with their web editor
4. Wait ~1–3 minutes for generation
5. Explore the world with their web viewer (WASD + mouse look)
6. Edit — move objects, change lighting, relight, paint over regions
7. Export:
   - **Gaussian splats** (`.ply` with Gaussian attributes, or their own format) — for real-time viewers like Luma, Polycam, or Three.js splat renderers
   - **Mesh** (GLB) — for Blender, Unity, Unreal, three.js
   - **Video** — rendered flythrough, for sharing and traditional post

Expect the export quality to be "good enough for previs and production dailies" rather than "final pixel ready for film." You will re-touch in Blender or Unreal.

## What we could build with it

The question with Marble isn't "what's possible" — it's "what becomes cheap enough to do casually that it changes the creative workflow." Some ideas:

- **Instant previs / storyboarding.** Describe a scene in text, get a rough 3D previs in two minutes. Replace the mood board phase entirely.
- **Location scouting for indie film and music video.** "A moody 1970s diner at 3am" generated and explored in VR to plan shots before renting a real location.
- **AR/VR content pipeline.** Marble → glTF → WebXR or Meta Quest experience in an afternoon.
- **Game environment blockout.** Generate 20 candidate environments for a level, pick one, then hand-polish it in Unreal. Massive time save on concept.
